answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Spoken by the character Francisco d’Anconia in his “money speech” in Rand’s novel Atlas Shrugged (Random House, 1957), Part Two, Chapter Two, “The Aristocracy of Pull.” Wikiquote cites p. 413 of the 1957 hardcover, and a reprint of the speech authorized by the Rand estate matches the popular wording word for word.

source.heading: Where it comes from

docMeta.dd: Part Two (“Either-Or”), Chapter Two, “The Aristocracy of Pull”; p. 413 in the 1957 hardcover (per Wikiquote)
Francisco d’Anconia (a character in the novel)

source.excerpt: “Do you wish to know whether that day is coming? Watch money. Money is the barometer of a society’s virtue. When you see that trading is done, not by consent, but by compulsion—when you see that in order to produce, you need to obtain permission from men who produce nothing—when you see that money is flowing to those who deal, not in goods, but in favors—when you see that men get richer by graft and by pull than by work, and your laws don’t protect you against them, but protect them against you—when you see corruption being rewarded and honesty becoming a self-sacrifice—you may know that your society is doomed. Money is so noble a medium that it does not compete with guns and it does not make terms with brutality. It will not permit a country to survive as half-property, half-loot.”
trail: Wikiquote’s Atlas Shrugged page ↗ lists the line under Part Two, Chapter Two, “The Aristocracy of Pull.” It cites p. 413 of the 1957 Random House hardcover and gives Francisco d’Anconia as the speaker.

Capitalism Magazine’s reprint of the speech ↗ is labeled “an excerpt from Atlas Shrugged, © Copyright, 1957, by Ayn Rand,” and was published by permission of her estate. It contains the exact wording, directly after “Money is the barometer of a society’s virtue.”
An editorial note in the Ayn Rand Institute’s letters archive ↗ says the speech was reprinted in Rand’s For the New Intellectual as “The Meaning of Money.”
The Quote Investigator articles tagged Ayn Rand ↗ do not cover this passage, so no specialist finding disagrees with the novel’s text.

Quoting a short passage for commentary is a separate fair-use question.

author.name: Ayn Rand
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.bio: Born Alisa Zinovyevna Rosenbaum in Saint Petersburg, Ayn Rand became a novelist and philosopher in the United States, best known for The Fountainhead and Atlas Shrugged. She founded the philosophy she called Objectivism. Atlas Shrugged was her last novel and the one she regarded as her fiction masterpiece.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The passage is part of a long speech in Atlas Shrugged. Francisco d’Anconia gives it at a party after a guest remarks that money is “the root of all evil” (Atlas Society ↗). It sits in a chapter Rand titled “The Aristocracy of Pull.” Historian Jennifer Burns notes that this chapter is about connections and favors pushing out merit (Burns, Journal of Cultural Economy, 2011 ↗).

The words belong to a fictional character, but Rand stood behind them in her own name. Burns notes that Rand reprinted the speech, under the new title “The Meaning of Money,” in her first nonfiction collection, For the New Intellectual (1961). Burns concludes that the speech can be read as a direct statement of Rand’s own views. That is why the list of warning signs, quoted on its own, is so often credited simply to “Ayn Rand.”
